idiom_name: single-branch precondition check followed by an immediate exit
implementation_notes: Language-neutral recipe: state each precondition as a positive requirement, test it at the top of the callable, and leave the body immediately when it fails - return, throw, or break/continue in a loop - using the failure shape the caller's contract expects. Put the checks before any resource acquisition and before the first mutation, so an exit cannot leave partial work behind, and order them from cheapest to most expensive. The classic nested-if form is still right in two cases: when the condition binds data the happy path needs (the else branch is not a pure rejection), and when the failure branch does substantive work such as logging plus compensation. Where the language offers a contract facility for programmer errors distinct from input validation, use it for that category and keep explicit guards for anything a caller can cause.
code_sketch:
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    if src is None or dst is None: raise InvalidArgument(...)   # guard: bad input
    if amount <= 0: raise InvalidArgument('amount')             # guard: one requirement
    if src.balance < amount: raise InsufficientFunds(...)       # guard: impossible state
    src.debit(amount)          # happy path stays flat, one level deep
    dst.credit(amount)
pitfalls: A guard that performs work before the exit - mutating, acquiring, logging state - makes the rejection observable and leaves the caller with a half-applied change.
Negated compound conditions invert the logic twice: name the requirement and test one simple expression, never a De Morgan puzzle.
Duplicated guards drift: the same precondition checked in callers and callee eventually disagrees; keep one owner for the check.
